units.title: Unit 91 — Adverbs
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 188–189 (PDF pages 189–190).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Adverbs of frequency, degree and manner
learningObjectives: Use common frequency adverbs along a scale from always to never.
Place frequency adverbs before main verbs, after be, and after the auxiliary in the present perfect.
Distinguish a bit, a little and slightly from quite, fairly, rather and pretty in degrees of intensity.
Use completely, totally, extremely and incredibly to express very strong degrees.
Choose manner adverbs that describe how an action happens, including quietly, secretly, urgently and politely.

items.example: I always check my bag before leaving home.
items.note: The highest frequency on the scale; it normally goes before a main verb.

items.example: Our neighbours often walk their dog in the evening.
items.note: Normally placed before a main verb but after the verb be.

items.example: The bus frequently arrives late on Fridays.
items.note: Similar in meaning to often; its position can vary in some clauses.

items.example: My brother quite often calls on Sunday evenings.
items.note: More frequent than sometimes, without suggesting always.

items.example: We sometimes have lunch in the park.
items.note: Means on some occasions, not every time.

items.example: I occasionally work from a cafe.
items.note: Less frequent than often; can also appear at the start of a sentence.

items.example: She hardly ever eats breakfast before work.
items.note: Very low frequency; do not add not to make a negative.

items.example: We rarely travel in the winter.
items.note: Low frequency; similar in meaning to hardly ever and seldom.

items.example: He seldom uses cash nowadays.
items.note: A rather formal alternative to rarely or hardly ever.

items.example: They never leave the office before six.
items.note: Zero frequency; already negative in meaning, so do not normally add not.

items.example: We see our old neighbours quite frequently.
items.note: Similar in meaning to quite often.

items.example: The shop is often busy after lunch.
items.note: Frequency adverbs normally come after forms of be.

items.example: I have never visited Scotland.
items.note: In the present perfect, never follows the auxiliary have or has.

items.example: I frequently visit my cousins at weekends.
items.note: A frequency adverb normally goes before a lexical or main verb.

items.example: I was a bit worried about the delay.
items.note: Informal modifier, commonly used before an adjective with a slightly negative meaning.

items.example: The room was a little cold in the morning.
items.note: A mild degree modifier before a predicative adjective.

items.example: The journey was a little bit longer than expected.
items.note: A slightly longer way to express a small degree; often informal.

items.example: She looked slightly nervous before the interview.
items.note: A small degree; unlike a bit, it can modify an adjective before a noun.

items.example: The restaurant was quite busy on Friday.
items.note: In the moderate-degree use here, stronger than a bit and usually weaker than very.

items.example: The instructions were fairly clear.
items.note: A moderate degree; used in positive or negative descriptions.

items.example: I was rather disappointed with the result.
items.note: A moderate degree; can express a slightly surprising or negative judgement.

items.example: The test was pretty difficult.
items.note: An informal adverb of degree, not the adjective meaning attractive.

items.example: The room was completely empty when we arrived.
items.note: Expresses a total degree; often interchangeable with totally.

items.example: I totally agree with your suggestion.
items.note: A strong degree of completeness; often interchangeable with completely.

items.example: It was an extremely interesting exhibition.
items.note: A very strong intensifier, stronger than quite or fairly.

items.example: The documentary was incredibly good.
items.note: Emphatic degree adverb meaning extremely.

items.example: I felt a bit tired after the train journey.
items.note: A natural use of a bit with a mildly negative state.

items.example: I was slightly nervous before meeting the team.
items.note: A mild description; slightly can appear before an adjective inside a noun phrase.

items.example: They rented a slightly small flat near the centre.
items.note: Slightly can modify an adjective before a noun; a bit cannot be used there in the same structure.

items.example: The hotel gave us quite a nice room.
items.note: With a noun phrase, the word order is quite + a/an + adjective + noun.

items.example: We had a fairly wet day during the trip.
items.note: Fairly appears between the article and adjective before a noun.

items.pt: uma festa até que muito boa; uma festa bastante boa
items.example: It turned out to be rather a good party.
items.note: Both rather a good party and a rather good party are possible.

items.example: Your first draft is pretty good.
items.note: An informal positive evaluation; degree is usually moderate to strong.

items.example: The car park was completely empty at dawn.
items.note: Completely naturally intensifies an absolute state such as empty.

items.example: I totally agree with the final decision.
items.note: Common strong-agreement phrase.

items.example: The reception desk was extremely busy this afternoon.
items.note: A strong degree of busy; contrasted in the practice activities.

items.example: The local cafe makes incredibly good cakes.
items.note: Incredibly can strongly emphasise a positive adjective.

items.example: Working until six is fairly typical in that office.
items.note: A moderate degree expression appearing in the personal practice task.

items.example: Her decision was slightly unusual but sensible.
items.note: A small difference from what is usual; from the reflection task.

items.example: It is quite unusual to see snow here in April.
items.note: Stronger than slightly unusual in the degree scale.

items.example: They secretly arranged a birthday meal for their friend.
items.note: Describes doing something without other people knowing about it.

items.example: She quietly closed the bedroom door.
items.note: Describes an action done without making much noise.

items.example: The lights suddenly went out during the meeting.
items.note: Describes an unexpected change occurring quickly.

items.example: The office urgently needs a replacement printer.
items.note: Something must be done quickly because it is important.

items.example: I briefly spoke to the director after lunch.
items.note: For a short time, or using only a few words.

items.example: He politely asked the driver to wait.
items.note: In a respectful and socially appropriate way.

items.example: She angrily refused to answer the question.
items.note: In a way that shows anger.

items.example: Please ask politely if you need more time.
items.note: Manner adverbs can follow a verb or come before an infinitive phrase.

items.example: The manager will speak briefly before the event.
items.note: Means speak for a short period; contrast with speaking quietly.

items.example: He reacted angrily to the unexpected criticism.
items.note: A verb + manner adverb collocation; the adverb describes the reaction.

sectionsChecked: A: Frequency scale and placement of adverbs with be and present perfect
B: Degree expressions, intensifiers, adjective position and register
C: Adverbs of manner in narrative captions and short situations
Exercises 91.1–91.5 including personalised frequency and degree practice

units.title: Unit 92 — Time and sequence
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 190–191 (PDF pages 191–192).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Time expressions, ordering events, and connecting reasons
learningObjectives: Distinguish when from as soon as and use present forms in future-time subordinate clauses.
Use while, as and just as to describe simultaneous actions and their timing.
Connect consecutive events with then, after that, afterwards, after and before, using the correct -ing construction.
Order actions with first, first of all and finally, and differentiate at first from eventually and in the end.
Add reasons with firstly, secondly, for one thing, for a start, besides and anyway.

items.section: A · When and as soon as
items.example: I will call you when the train arrives.
items.note: A time conjunction. In future-time clauses, use the present form after when, not will.

items.section: A · When and as soon as
items.example: We will leave as soon as the rain stops.
items.note: Suggests that the next action follows immediately or is especially important.

items.section: A · When and as soon as
items.example: I will email the photos when I get home.
items.note: A future meaning expressed using the present simple after when.

items.section: A · When and as soon as
items.example: I will send you a message as soon as I arrive.
items.note: Use present simple in the time clause even if the main clause refers to the future.

items.section: A · When and as soon as
items.example: You can go home when you have finished the task.
items.note: Present perfect can follow when when the completion of an earlier action matters.

items.section: B · Actions at the same time
items.example: I made lunch while my sister set the table.
items.note: Often links two activities happening over a period of time.

items.section: B · Actions at the same time
items.example: I saw an old friend as I left the office.
items.note: In this unit, as can connect events that happen at the same time.

items.pt: exatamente quando; bem no momento em que
items.section: B · Actions at the same time
items.example: The phone rang just as I closed my laptop.
items.note: Emphasises the coincidence of two short actions.

items.section: B · Actions at the same time
items.example: Both groups arrived at the same time.
items.note: Indicates that two actions or events occur together.

items.section: B · Actions at the same time
items.example: I read the news while I was waiting for the bus.
items.note: The past continuous describes the longer activity during another event.

items.section: B · Actions at the same time
items.example: Listen to a podcast while cooking dinner.
items.note: A shorter while + -ing clause is possible when the subject is understood.

items.pt: bem na hora em que eu saí
items.section: B · Actions at the same time
items.example: I met my neighbour just as I left the building.
items.note: Useful for two actions that coincide at a precise moment.

items.example: We finished breakfast, then went for a walk.
items.note: Connects the next action in a sequence.

items.example: The meeting ended, and after that we went for coffee.
items.note: Introduces the next event in a sequence; often interchangeable with then.

items.example: I visited the museum and afterwards met my friends.
items.note: An adverb meaning at a later time, often later the same day.

items.example: After dinner, we sat outside and talked.
items.note: A preposition or conjunction; after may be followed by a noun or an -ing form.

items.example: Wash your hands before lunch.
items.note: A preposition or conjunction; before may be followed by a noun or an -ing form.

items.example: We went shopping after finishing work.
items.note: Use after + -ing, not after + the bare infinitive.

items.pt: antes de sair; antes de partir
items.example: We checked the windows before leaving.
items.note: Use before + -ing when an action comes before another one.

items.example: I made a few notes after my visit.
items.note: A common after + noun phrase expressing later time.

items.example: We had something to eat before going out.
items.note: A natural before + -ing expression for a prior action.

items.example: First, check that the door is locked.
items.note: Introduces the first action or instruction in a sequence.

items.pt: antes de tudo; primeiro de tudo
items.example: First of all, we need to choose a date.
items.note: Introduces the first action in an ordered account.

items.example: Finally, we returned home after the trip.
items.note: Introduces the last item in an ordered series; different from eventually.

items.example: Write the events in the correct sequence.
items.note: A series of actions that happen one after another.

items.example: To begin with, the lessons seemed difficult.
items.note: Here it describes the initial stage of a situation; it can also introduce a first point.

items.example: At first I disliked the course, but now I enjoy it.
items.note: Describes the beginning of a situation that changes later; not a simple synonym for first in a sequence.

items.pt: depois de um tempo; passado algum tempo
items.example: After a while, she began to feel more relaxed.
items.note: Signals that some time has passed before the next event.

items.pt: por fim; finalmente; depois de algum tempo
items.example: We searched for an hour and eventually found the address.
items.note: Means finally after a long time, difficulty, or several events; not merely possibly.

items.pt: no fim das contas; por fim; afinal
items.example: In the end, I decided to stay in my current job.
items.note: Signals the final outcome after some thought or time; contrast with finally for the last item in a list.

items.example: Firstly, the rent is too high.
items.note: Introduces the first reason in an ordered argument.

items.example: Secondly, the flat is too far from work.
items.note: Adds a second reason after firstly.

items.pt: por um lado; para começar; em primeiro lugar
items.example: For one thing, I have an appointment that evening.
items.note: Introduces one of several reasons in a conversational argument.

items.example: For a start, we cannot afford a new car.
items.note: Conversational way to introduce the first reason; similar to for one thing.

items.example: I am tired, and besides, the tickets are expensive.
items.note: Adds another supporting reason to what has just been said.

items.pt: além disso; de qualquer forma; de todo modo
items.example: The trip is expensive, and anyway, I cannot take time off.
items.note: Here adds another consideration; it can also mean in any case or mark a topic change.

sectionsChecked: A: When / As soon as and the future-time grammar warning
B: Simultaneous actions with while, as and just as
C: Subsequent events with then, after that, afterwards, after and before
D: Action sequences using first of all, first, then and finally
E: At first, to begin with, after a while, eventually and in the end
Exercises 92.1–92.4 with synonym matching, verb forms, dialogue completions and free responses
